extracted.intended_audience: general readers, especially American parents, homemakers, and domestic moralists (late 19th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on temperance, household music, family religion, boy upbringing, and cookery — advice aimed at parents and housewives about how to cultivate moral, musical, and domestic habits in the home.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance: restrict sale and social encouragement of alcohol
rubrics_metrics.description: Had I my way, not one drop of intoxicating liquors should be sold, except by druggists, and then only by a physician's prescription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author holds that pure brandy, wine and whiskey have inestimable value as medicine and acknowledges judicious restorative uses, but opposes their common sale and the social encouragement of drinking. She warns against lending any aid (even social pressure or holding a glass) to another's indulgence: 'Woe unto him that putteth the cup to his neighbor's lips!' and condemns 'mistaken toleration of good people' toward intemperance. Examples of ruin (families destroyed by rum) are cited as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance: avoid exposing susceptible persons to stimulants
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no sin or even danger in the occasional use of them in the kitchen...but if one of her family or guests already loves and craves the stimulant, it is prudent to omit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooking uses (a tablespoonful of wine in pudding-sauce or a wineglassful in jelly) do not make a drunkard, but prudence requires omission if any family member is already tempted. The household should not give 'the final touch' that may complete inebriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family music: encourage communal singing and amateur participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Households should make and use collections of vocal music; once nearly every household sang by note and every member took part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts past widespread sight-singing and family part-songs with a modern tendency to place music solely in professionals' hands. She argues that home music — simple tunes, ballads, part-songs — builds happy homes and communal enjoyment. Anti-pattern: letting one 'privileged' musician dominate and discourage amateur participation; being hypercritical to the point of silencing others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical education for the masses: value of singing-school and basic training
rubrics_metrics.description: The singing-school and basic training in intervals/gamut cultivated the national ear; such instruction made general appreciation of music possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends restoring widespread elementary musical instruction so that many can sing and appreciate music intelligently. She cites German practice of cultivating ear and voice from childhood as a model. Guidance: teach basic sight-singing and ballads so all can join; resist confining music only to expensive private instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose elitist, hypercritical musical cults that silence amateurs
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Wagner cult' and similar dogmas make people demand 'music that has a tune in it' seem like a triviality; professionals becoming intolerant of amateur work is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When trained musicians become disdainful, they suppress home music. The remedy: encourage detection of promise and encouragement of tyros (novices) rather than scorn; value simple tunes and communal singing over exclusive taste-showing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family religion: parents as primary religious instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The church which is in thy house' should be a living reality; early family devotions (grace before meat, family Bible study, catechism) must not be sacrificed to convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author, claiming long experience as a Bible-class teacher, insists mothers and fathers are responsible for children's familiarity with Scripture and doctrine. Practices recommended: regular family prayer, weekly study of Sunday-school lessons at home (using references, concordance, Bible dictionary), committing Psalms and New Testament passages to memory, and treating the home as the primary 'nursery of the church.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not delegate children's spiritual formation to Sunday-school alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sunday-school, originally for neglected children, has been made the chief instrument relied on by well-to-do members for the spiritual upbuilding of their children — a mistaken delegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes the 'contract system' where teachers/organizations do the work while parents expect no preparation from children. She urges parental engagement: preparation of lessons at home, parental presence in children's religious instruction, and resisting the idea that two services excuse family devotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious instruction: value of disciplined, repeated Scripture reading and memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading through the Bible yearly, committing Psalms and gospels to memory, and repeated close contact with Scripture produces long-lasting spiritual resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author defends 'primitive methods' (annual Bible readings and rote learning) as forming memory and imagination with Holy Writ, producing phrases and consolations that last a lifetime. She compares this to Demosthenes' repeated translations to inform style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church and worship: include and cultivate children's participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should not be excluded from worship; parental habits that push them out of the pew undermine reverence and veneration for church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that early habit of keeping children out of services leads to their later disrespect for church authority and development of parallel youth organizations. Parents should accept the inconvenience and include children so they learn to find worship 'amiable' and venerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boy upbringing: provide equitable, dignified lodgings for boys
rubrics_metrics.description: Boys should be given a domain in which they can feel pride of proprietorship — not relegated to shabby back-rooms while sisters have fitted chambers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unequal lodging breeds humiliation and alienation; parents should maintain the 'just mean' between pampering daughters and neglecting sons. Furnishings should express maternal love and be appropriate to his station and education. Anti-pattern: keeping the boy's quarters sunless, shabby, or placed with servants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boy upbringing: respect individuality; allow controlled disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the boy have his 'den' and do not rigidly invade his individuality; clean and bright are necessary, but avoid meddling with his books/papers which mark his identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: tidy the glaring disorders but do not purge every personal mark; avoid rigid surveillance that would 'irk him.' The mother should preserve his imprint to foster selfhood; gifts and tasteful contributions to his quarters are seeds set in good soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental conduct: equality and visible expression of love matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners and environment harmonize; visible expressions of maternal devotion (well-appointed rooms, tasteful engravings) form children's taste and self-respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate right tastes by judicious dependence on external impressions: hang good engravings, provide tasteful surroundings. Avoid humiliating comparisons between siblings' accommodations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household cookery: balance economy with culinary art and flavor
rubrics_metrics.description: American cookery tends toward 'fillingness' and economy of time; French cookery prioritizes daintiness and flavor — the household should value both nourishment and taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author encourages recognizing cooking as an art where small extra effort (e.g., a good soup stock made from cracked bones and vegetables simmered slowly) yields nourishing dinners without wasting time or fuel. She criticizes the national prejudice against soups, jellies, salads and entrées as 'danger-signals' to quick-housewives, and recommends moderate investment in such dishes for better food quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cookery: use economical labor-saving preparations wisely (stock and simple desserts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A few pounds of cracked bones, vegetables and herbs set to simmer will make stock that is the base of many nourishing dinners; simple desserts like blanc-mange or Spanish cream can be made quickly and cheaply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate by example that these preparations save time and fuel while improving meals; favor economical, nutritious options over laborious but inferior pies. The author suggests showing mathematical or practical proof to housewives who prize saving minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cookery: diversify beyond salted and preserved meats; use vegetables, fresh fish and salads
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on salt pork, salt beef, salt fish, and heavy 'filling' dishes leads to poor diet; Americans actually have abundant fresh vegetables, fruits, and fish that should be better utilized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage use of fresh produce and fish, salads with mayonnaise, and less dependence on preserved meats. Critiques cultural prejudices (e.g., sneering at salads) and recommends taking advantage of the country's superior raw materials.
